mcqs.question: Why is the IQR method often preferred over a z-score cutoff on data that isn't bell-shaped?
options: IQR is based on quartiles, so it's less distorted by extreme values and skewed distributions
IQR runs faster on very large datasets
IQR works across multiple features simultaneously, unlike z-score
IQR requires no assumptions about the number of anomalies present
mcqs.explanation: The z-score cutoff assumes a roughly normal distribution and can itself be skewed by extreme outliers pulling the mean and standard deviation; IQR relies on the median and quartiles, which resist that distortion. Both are single-feature methods and both are equally 'assumption-free' about anomaly count.

mcqs.question: In an isolation forest, what does a very short average path length to isolate a point indicate?
options: The point is very close to the center of the normal data
The point is likely an anomaly, since it took few random splits to isolate
The forest needs more trees to be reliable
The point's features are all missing
mcqs.explanation: Isolation forest relies on the fact that outliers, sitting far from the bulk of normal data, get separated into their own leaf after very few random splits, while normal points require many more splits to isolate. A short path length is therefore the anomaly signal, not a sign of centrality.

mcqs.question: An anomaly detector on a dataset with 0.4% true anomalies reports 99.6% accuracy by flagging nothing at all. What does this reveal?
options: The detector is working correctly and needs no further evaluation
Accuracy is a misleading metric here, since a trivial always-normal predictor achieves nearly the same score
99.6% accuracy proves recall on the anomaly class is also high
mcqs.explanation: With a 0.4% positive rate, predicting 'normal' for everything already scores 99.6% accuracy while catching zero anomalies — the metric says nothing about real detection performance. Precision and recall on the anomaly class are needed to see the actual trade-off.

mcqs.question: Why is the anomaly-score cutoff typically chosen based on the cost of false positives versus false negatives, rather than a fixed statistical rule like a z-score of 3?
options: A z-score of 3 is mathematically invalid for anomaly scores in general

The cost of missing a real anomaly and the cost of a false alarm are usually very different in practice, so the threshold that minimizes actual business cost rarely lines up with a generic statistical cutoff
Statistical thresholds only apply to supervised classification, not anomaly detection
Business costs are impossible to quantify, so any threshold choice is equally arbitrary
mcqs.explanation: A generic cutoff like z-score of 3 treats both error types as equally costly, which is rarely true — missing real fraud usually costs far more than an analyst clearing a false alarm. The threshold that actually minimizes cost is found by weighing the two error rates against their real costs along the precision-recall curve, not by defaulting to a statistically 'natural' number.
